region: Southern Småland, in the forest uplands
description: Mossaby is a poor forest parish in the Småland uplands, a scattering of small farms and crofts on stony ground between spruce forest, bogs and lakes. The fields are made by carrying stones off them for generations, piled in long walls through the woods. Since the famine years at the end of the 1860s, families have been leaving for America almost every month, and empty cottages stand with their doors nailed shut.
seasonNotes: October. The rowans are red with berries and the birches yellow against dark spruce, but the stony fields have given a thin harvest again. Mists lie over the bogs each morning and rise slowly through the trees. Potatoes are being dug and stored, and lingonberries picked in the forest. The rains come and the stream rises enough for the mill to grind. The days grow short and cold, and the first frost blackens the potato tops.
travel: Uppsala by rail to Stockholm, then by the Stockholm-Katrineholm line and the Southern Main Line to Nässjö (about twelve hours in all, with an overnight at Nässjö), then most of a day by hired carriage or farm cart on bad forest roads to Mossaby. In October the Göta Canal (via Mem and Berg, then rail from Linköping) is a slower alternative while the season lasts.

geography.realAnalogue: Älmeboda (Uppvidinge härad, Kronoberg), a poor emigration parish in the forest uplands of southern Småland
knownFor: Poor stony forest farms, and fields made by carrying stones off the land into long walls
Heavy emigration to America since the hunger years of 1867-68
Tar, charcoal and timber from the spruce forest
The wise man of the forest, consulted by three parishes about sick cattle and lost things

authorities.police: Kronolänsman of the Mossaby district, who is also tax collector and lives in the parish. He is the only law within a day's ride and keeps order, summons people to court and sends the reports on.
authorities.court: Häradsrätt for the Mossaby forest district, seated in Växjö, with a judge and twelve lay assessors. It sits at fixed times of the year, and people travel a long way to attend. Poaching, boundary quarrels and timber theft are the usual cases.
authorities.doctor: Provinsialläkare for the Småland forest district, seated in Växjö, a day or more away by farm cart. He is called only in grave cases, and he signs the death certificates.
authorities.post: A small post office at the church village. The post comes by carrier from Nässjö or Växjö about twice a week and goes out the same way. Emigrants' letters and tickets arrive by it.
authorities.telegraph: Nearest at Nässjö station, about 55 km north, and at Växjö. Telegrams are carried on by boy or cart, and a day is lost.
authorities.bank: Växjö sparbank in the county town, where crofters keep small savings. Smålands Enskilda Bank of Jönköping also deals in the area. The parish has no bank of its own, and the vicar and the richer farmers lend money.
authorities.newspaper: Smålandsposten of Växjö, founded 1865, which prints parish news, emigration notices and market prices. It reaches the parish by post a few days late.

routes.name: By rail to Nässjö, then hired carriage

legs.cost: roughly 2 to 3 riksdaler in second class (approximate)
legs.notes: Private standard-gauge line via Knivsta, Märsta and Rotebro. At Stockholm the passenger crosses town from the northern station to the southern one with luggage.
State trunk line via Södertälje and Gnesta. Passengers change at Katrineholm for the southern line, with a wait of an hour or two.

legs.schedule: one or two through trains a day
legs.notes: Southern Main Line via Mjölby and Linköping. The train from Stockholm usually arrives late in the evening, and travellers lodge at an inn in Nässjö. The line to Oskarshamn does not exist before 1874.

legs.duration: most of a day, 8 to 10 hours
legs.cost: roughly 10 to 14 riksdaler for a hired carriage and driver (approximate)
legs.schedule: on demand from the inn, with an early start
legs.notes: A bad forest road. In October it is full of ruts and mud, and one changes horses once at a roadside inn (skjutsstation). Hired horses are fewer in autumn at the threshing, so the order must be given the night before.

routes.name: By the Göta Canal and rail from Linköping, then farm cart

legs.cost: roughly 2 to 3 riksdaler in second class (approximate)

legs.duration: about a day and a night
legs.schedule: a few sailings a week in the open season
legs.notes: The Baltic steamer along the Södermanland and Östergötland coast to the canal's eastern mouth. No lineId is given for it in the period list, and it is a stretch of approximate canon. Autumn gales may delay it, and in October the boats thin out.

legs.duration: about a day and a night through the locks and Lake Roxen
legs.schedule: passenger steamers daily in the season, fewer in October
legs.notes: The canal is closed by ice outside the season, and in late October the last sailings are uncertain. A slow, cold route, but the hold is quiet and travellers can talk freely.
A short drive from the canal landing to Linköping station, on a good road.

legs.schedule: one or two trains a day
legs.notes: Southern Main Line via Mjölby. Travellers reach Nässjö in the evening and spend a night there.

legs.cost: roughly 4 to 6 riksdaler for a farmer's cart and a boy (approximate)
legs.schedule: farmers' carts go back on market days and after delivering goods; otherwise ask at the inn
legs.notes: The cheap way into the forest, slower than a hired carriage. The driver knows every farm on the road, and gossip is part of the fare. In October the road may be dark before the journey ends.

journey.journeyScene: The railway carries you through the Östergötland plain, fields gold and brown and wet, until the plain breaks into low hills and the first spruce stands close to the line. At Nässjö the lamps are lit, and railway men, timber dealers and a few families with trunks and tin-bound boxes wait for the next train to the port. The road into the forest begins at the first stone wall, which runs alongside for mile after mile and disappears into the spruce wood. By the time the cart reaches Mossaby it is nearly dark, and the autumn mist lies over the bogs and the lake. Rowan trees stand red by the gates, and the smell of peat smoke hangs from the cottages. Some of them have their doors nailed shut and their windows blind.”,

publicFacts: In the famine years of 1867 and 1868 the harvest failed twice and the parish went hungry; many sold their land.
Some forty people have left Mossaby for America in the last three years, most for Minnesota and Illinois; their letters and tickets arrive by post.
An emigration agent visits the parish twice a year selling passages via Gothenburg and Liverpool.
The vicar holds the household examination in each village in November and keeps careful records of who has gone.
The parish is crossed by stone walls built by generations of farmers clearing their fields.
A miller grinds at the stream mill only in autumn and spring, when there is enough water.
The revival preachers have a strong following in the parish, and many families hold devotions at home.
The wise man in the forest is visited by people from three parishes for sick animals and lost things.

places.name: Mossaby Church
places.description: The church is a small white building with a tarred wooden tower, standing on a hill of glacial gravel above the lake. The churchyard wall is built of the same grey stones as every field wall in the parish. Yellow birch leaves blow across the graves. Inside it smells of damp, and the plaster on the walls is cracked.

affordances.description: A small vaulted room off the chancel where the vicar robes.

affordances.name: Church loft

places.name: Mossaby Parsonage
places.ownerRole: the vicar of the parish, who lives here and serves the church
places.description: The parsonage is a plain red house with white corners, the best building in the parish though its roof leaks. Lingonberries are spread on cloths in the kitchen. The vicar works by lamplight early in the afternoon, adding notes of 'moved to North America' to the registers. The glebe fields around it are as stony as everyone else's.

places.ownerRole: a freeholder farming family; the farm is named for a great-grandmother, Ingeborg
places.description: A small farm on a slope above the lake, its grey timber house surrounded by birches and stone walls. The farmer and his sons are digging potatoes in the wet field. Smoke rises from the bathhouse where malt is drying. A pig is fattening in a pen for the slaughter.

places.name: Stenbacken
places.ownerRole: a crofter family preparing to leave for America
places.description: A tiny croft on a stony hill among the spruces, with a grey cottage and a byre for one cow. The family is preparing to leave for America in the spring, and the chest is already packed in the corner. Mist drips from the trees. The potato patch has been dug and only stones remain.

places.name: Rävmossen
places.ownerRole: a crofter family on the bog
places.description: The cottage stands at the edge of a wide bog, its windows dark, its door nailed shut since the family left for America last year. Nobody has bought it, and the meadow is going back to heather and birch scrub. The mist rolls in from the bog in the morning. A path of logs leads across the bog to the forest beyond.

places.name: Bäckakvarn
places.description: A small grey mill stands where the stream falls through a rocky gorge in the forest, its wheel turning now that the autumn rains have come. The water foams white over the stones and the noise fills the narrow valley. Moss and ferns cover every surface. The miller is an old man who grinds for half the parish in the few weeks the water lasts.

places.name: The Wise Man's Cottage
places.ownerRole: the wise man, a cunning man the parish both fears and needs
places.description: Deep in the forest, an hour's walk from any farm, a small cottage stands by a spring among old spruces. Bundles of plants and bark hang from every beam. A cat watches from the window. People come here from far away, though they rarely speak of it.

places.name: The Parish Smithy
places.description: The smithy stands at the crossroads in the middle of the parish, an old building of stone and timber. The smith makes scythes and axes for the forest farms and repairs the emigrants' trunks. The forge glows red in the grey autumn afternoon. Farmers stop there to talk and exchange news from America.
